questions.q: What does RLHF actually align the policy to?
options: A formal, hand-written specification of good behavior
Human preference labels, as captured by a learned reward model
An objective ground-truth reward signal
The original pretraining objective
questions.explain: RLHF optimizes the policy against a reward model trained on human preference comparisons. There is no independent, ground-truth signal of 'good' in the loop — only what the labels captured.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the structural limits of RLHF discussed in this lesson?
options: It cannot be implemented with any RL algorithm
Labeler disagreement on hard or value-laden questions produces a noisy, averaged preference signal
It only works on vision models, not language models
It removes the need for any reward signal at all
questions.explain: Human raters frequently disagree, especially on ambiguous or contested questions, so the reward model ends up learning an average over noisy and sometimes contradictory judgments.

questions.q: Why does RLHF face a scalability ceiling as models approach or exceed human-level performance on a task?
options: Reward models cannot be trained using preference comparisons
Human raters can't reliably judge outputs on tasks that exceed their own expertise
RLHF can only be applied to short text responses
Reward models require infinite training data to function at all
questions.explain: A confident, fluent, wrong answer can look as good as or better than a correct one to a rater who can't evaluate the task. That caps how far human judgment can reliably scale as a training signal.

questions.q: What is the key mechanical difference between RLHF and RLAIF?
options: RLAIF discards the reward model entirely and uses rule-based scoring
RLAIF replaces some or all human preference labels with AI-generated judgments, while keeping the same RL mechanics
RLAIF requires no policy optimization step
RLAIF only applies to image-generation models
questions.explain: RLAIF keeps the reward-model-plus-policy-optimization structure of RLHF, but an AI model (as in Constitutional AI) supplies some or all of the preference comparisons instead of a human rater.

questions.q: Does substituting AI feedback for human feedback (RLAIF) eliminate RLHF's structural limits?
options: Yes — an AI judge is immune to disagreement and can evaluate any task correctly
No — it scales the labeling process, but an AI judge can still be noisy, still face a version of the scalability ceiling, and the method still only shapes surface behavior
Yes — because the written constitution replaces the need for any judgment at all
No — because RLAIF cannot be combined with reinforcement learning
questions.explain: RLAIF makes preference data much cheaper to produce, but it doesn't resolve what RLHF was structurally unable to guarantee — the limits relocate to the AI judge rather than disappearing.
